reference.source: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology / Shields' Textbook of Glaucoma
clinicalPearls: A form of angle closure in which anteriorly positioned ciliary processes push the peripheral iris forward to crowd or close the angle, rather than pupillary block being the main mechanism
The central anterior chamber is typically of normal or near-normal depth, but the peripheral iris rises steeply and then flattens, giving a plateau-like profile
It should be suspected when angle closure persists or recurs despite a patent laser peripheral iridotomy
The term plateau iris configuration describes the anatomy, while plateau iris syndrome denotes residual appositional angle closure after iridotomy has relieved any pupillary-block component
Anterior segment imaging with ultrasound biomicroscopy characteristically shows anteriorly rotated ciliary processes supporting the peripheral iris
Dilation can precipitate angle closure by bunching the peripheral iris into the crowded angle
Management after iridotomy may include laser peripheral iridoplasty to contract and flatten the peripheral iris away from the angle, with topical agents and long-term monitoring
It tends to occur in younger patients than typical pupillary-block angle closure
reference.pathophysiology: In plateau iris the ciliary body and its processes sit abnormally far forward, mechanically supporting and displacing the peripheral iris towards the trabecular meshwork so that the angle is crowded. The central anterior chamber remains reasonably deep because the mechanism is peripheral rather than a generalised forward shift of the iris-lens diaphragm. A relative pupillary-block element may coexist, which a laser peripheral iridotomy relieves; when appositional angle closure persists despite a patent iridotomy, the residual peripheral crowding from the anteriorly placed ciliary processes defines plateau iris syndrome. Pupil dilation worsens the situation by folding the peripheral iris into the already narrow angle, and chronic apposition can lead to peripheral anterior synechiae and pressure elevation.
additionalDifferentials: Primary angle-closure glaucoma from pupillary block
Phacomorphic angle closure from a large lens
Angle closure from a ciliary body cyst or tumour
Secondary angle closure from posterior segment pushing mechanisms
Narrow angle from a small hypermetropic eye
additionalInvestigations: Gonioscopy, including indentation gonioscopy, before and after iridotomy to demonstrate persistent peripheral apposition
Ultrasound biomicroscopy or anterior segment OCT to show anteriorly positioned ciliary processes
Applanation tonometry to detect pressure elevation
Assessment of central anterior chamber depth to distinguish it from generalised shallowing
OCT of the optic nerve and perimetry to monitor for glaucomatous damage
Provocative or post-dilation angle assessment where appropriate
redFlags: Persistent or recurrent appositional angle closure despite a patent iridotomy
Acute pressure rise precipitated by pupil dilation
Progressive peripheral anterior synechiae and rising pressure
Optic-nerve damage from unrecognised chronic angle closure
reference.prognosis: With recognition and treatment, including iridotomy and iridoplasty where needed, angle closure is often controlled and the prognosis is good, but unrecognised plateau iris can cause progressive synechial closure and glaucomatous damage requiring ongoing surveillance and sometimes further intervention.
pitfalls: Assuming a patent iridotomy has resolved the angle closure without repeating gonioscopy
Failing to image the ciliary processes and missing the true mechanism
Dilating the pupil and precipitating an acute rise
Confusing the deep central chamber with a normal angle and overlooking peripheral crowding
Not distinguishing plateau iris syndrome from malignant glaucoma, which needs very different treatment
management: Perform laser peripheral iridotomy first to eliminate any coexisting pupillary-block component
Add argon laser peripheral iridoplasty to flatten and retract the peripheral iris when appositional angle closure persists despite a patent iridotomy
Use a miotic such as pilocarpine to keep the pupil constricted and prevent peripheral iris bunching into the angle
Avoid pharmacological mydriasis and counsel against dilating agents that can precipitate angle closure
Lower intraocular pressure with topical agents such as prostaglandin analogues, beta-blockers or carbonic anhydrase inhibitors as needed, and consider lens extraction where the lens contributes
Maintain surveillance with gonioscopy, tonometry, optic nerve assessment and perimetry to detect synechial closure and glaucomatous damage
Refer to ophthalmology or a glaucoma specialist and escalate for progressive or uncontrolled angle closure
